title: 道德經 第五十九章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 59, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 82. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 59 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 守道 (Guarding the Way). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

morph.gloss: to govern, to bring into order
men, people — those a ruler has charge of
to serve, to attend upon — the noun 'an affair, business' put to work as a verb
nothing, none — a negative that carries its own subject inside it
to be the like of, to match
sparing — holding back and using little; at root the farmer's reaping and laying by (the same word as 穡)

sentences.l:
Governing men, serving heaven —
nothing is the like of sparing.
sentences.i: For ruling men and serving heaven there is nothing like being sparing.
sentences.n:
莫若 is the classical superlative. 莫 is a negative with its own subject already in it — 'nothing, no one' — so 莫若嗇 is 'nothing is the equal of sparing'. You met the same 莫 in chapter 32's 天下莫能臣, 'no one under heaven can make a subject of it'.

嗇 is the chapter's word and it is not quite 'thrift'. Its root is agricultural: grain taken in and stored, the same word as 穡 'to reap and lay by'. Wang Bi glosses it flatly — 嗇，農夫, 'sparing is the farmer', who clears his field of whatever does not belong there and does nothing in a hurry.

事天 is read two ways and the Chinese settles neither: the ruler serving Heaven, with the sacrifices that were his office, or any man tending the heaven-given nature he was born with. This chapter is also one of the handful expounded in the Han Feizi's 解老 (3rd c. BC), which makes these lines among the earliest of the book to be quoted anywhere outside it.

morph.gloss: now, as for — the particle that opens a general pronouncement (fú, not fū 'a grown man')
only, precisely — 夫唯 X is a fixed opening, 'it is just X and nothing else'
early-submitting — giving in to the way of things before anything forces you to; Wang Bi expands it as 早服其常, submitting early to what abides
to submit, to yield, to give oneself over to — the verb behind the noun 服 'clothing', what one puts on and wears

sentences.l:
Now, only sparing —
this is called early-submitting.
sentences.i: It is sparing, and nothing else, that is called submitting early.
sentences.n:
是謂 'this is called' christens a term, and a phrase the text names outright is a word the reader learns whole — so 早服 is one tap-unit here, and the next unit picks it up as a subject in its own right. The same naming made 玄牝 a word in chapter 6 and 襲明 one in chapter 27.

服 is the verb that stands behind the noun 'clothing': to put a thing on, to take it on, hence to submit to it and serve under it. (In the Mawangdui silk manuscripts 早 is regularly written 蚤 'flea', borrowed for its sound alone; where that graph turns up, this is the word.)

morph.gloss: it — an OBJECT PRONOUN here, not the genitive 'of'
weightily, deep-laid — a heavy, unhurried piling-up (zhòng)
to heap up, to store up, as grain is stored in a barn
potency — the power a thing has by being what it is

sentences.l: Early-submitting — call it weighty heaping-up of potency.
sentences.i: To submit early is to lay potency up deep.
sentences.n:
謂之: 之 is the object pronoun, 'call it'. Three units further down (有國之母) the same character will be the genitive 'of'. One character, two jobs, no ending to tell them apart — only position does.

重 is a polyphone and this line is a genuine toss-up. Read zhòng it is 'weighty, deep-laid', potency piled up with the gravity of chapter 26's 重為輕根, 'the heavy is the root of the light'. Read chóng it is 'again and again', layer upon layer. We take zhòng, because Wang Bi sets 重積德 against 銳速, 'sharp and quick' — the thing being opposed is haste, and weight is what opposes it. The sense barely moves either way.

sentences.t:
重積德則無不克，
無不克則莫知其極；

morph.gloss: then, and in that case — it introduces the consequence
there is not, there is nothing
to overcome, to master, to prove equal to
its — the Chinese does not say whose; see the note
the far limit — properly the ridgepole at the peak of a roof, the highest point there is

sentences.l:
Weighty heaping-up of potency, and then there is nothing not overcome;
nothing not overcome, and then no one knows its limit.
sentences.i: Lay potency up deep, and there is nothing you cannot overcome; and if there is nothing you cannot overcome, no one can find the limit of it.
sentences.n:
無不克 is a double negative used as an absolute: 'there is nothing that is not overcome'. Classical Chinese reaches for this where English would simply say 'everything' — and it is worth noticing that the sentence names no one who does the overcoming. It does not need to.

其極, 'its limit' — whose, the Chinese does not say. Wang Bi answers in three characters, 道無窮也, 'the Way is without end', taking the limitlessness to be the Way's own; read straight on from the line before, it is the limit of the potency the ruler has piled up. The English leaves it open, as the Chinese does.

From here the chapter climbs a ladder, each rung taking up the whole of the one before it as its own first term: A 則 B, B 則 C, then C 可以 D. The English repeats the phrases word for word wherever the Chinese repeats the characters — nothing is repeated for ornament, the repetition is the argument.

sentences.t:
莫知其極，
可以有國；

morph.gloss: its — see the note to the unit before
by that means, thereby — the object of 以 is left unsaid
to have, to hold, to possess
a state, a ruler's realm — a walled capital and the land it holds

sentences.l:
No one knows its limit —
by that one may hold a state.
sentences.i: When no one can find that limit, you can hold a state.
sentences.n:
可以 is two words, not one: 可 'can' and 以 'by that means', with the means itself left unstated. English swallows both into a bare 'can'.

Wang Bi supplies the reason: 以有窮而蒞國，非能有國也 — 'to preside over a state with something that has an end to it is not really to hold the state.'

This chapter rhymes hard, and Mandarin has eaten nearly all of it. 嗇, 服, 德, 克, 極 and 國 all belonged to one Old Chinese rhyme group — the one traditionally named 職 — so the five units you have just read chimed on a single sound six times over. In Mandarin they come out sè, fú, dé, kè, jí, guó: dé and kè still answer each other, and the rest have scattered.

sentences.t:
有國之母，
可以長久；

morph.gloss: of (the genitive — the same character that was 'it' three units ago)
mother — what a thing is born from and goes on being fed by; Wang Bi: 'what keeps a state secure is called its mother'
enduring, lasting long (of time, not of length)

sentences.l:
Holding the mother of the state —
by that one may be long and enduring.
sentences.i: Hold the mother of the state, and you may last long.
sentences.n:
The line divides two ways and the unpunctuated text chooses neither. Take 國之母 together and it is 'the mother of the state' — hold that, and you last. Take 有國 together and it is 'the mother of holding a state', the thing that makes possession possible in the first place. Wang Bi glosses 國之所以安謂之母, 'what a state is kept secure by is called its mother', which leans to the first; the English above follows him, and the two readings end in much the same place.

母 and 久 belonged to one Old Chinese rhyme group, and here — rarely — you can still half-hear it: mǔ, jiǔ.

sentences.t:
是謂深根固柢，
長生久視之道。

morph.gloss: to make deep, to drive deep — the adjective 'deep' doing a verb's work
root — the spread of roots a plant puts out
to make firm, to fix fast — again an adjective used as a verb
the taproot, the root-stock a tree stands on — the single root that goes straight down
to look, to keep one's eyes on (the looking; 見 is the seeing that results)

sentences.l:
This is called deepening the root and firming the taproot,
the way of long living and enduring seeing.
sentences.i: This is called driving the root deep and setting the taproot fast — the way to live long and to go on looking.
sentences.n:
深 and 固 are adjectives put to work as verbs: 'deepen the root', 'make the taproot fast'. Nothing in the words marks the change — position does, and this is one of the language's standing moves.

根 and 柢 are not the same thing. 根 is the spreading root, 柢 the single stock a tree stands on; English has no neat pair, so the literal takes 'root' and 'taproot'.

長生 and 久視 are built alike — long + live, long + look — and 久視 is the odd one. To go on looking is to go on being there to see. Both phrases were later seized on by the Daoist longevity movements as technical terms for physical deathlessness; that is not yet what they are doing here. They stay two words apiece for the same reason: the parallel is the point, and it disappears if either is glued shut.

The comma before 長生久視之道 is an editor's, like every mark in this text. Without it 之道 governs both pairs at once — 'the way of deep root and firm taproot, of long life and lasting sight' — and the sense hardly moves.
